## What the search found

There is no single "quickest" sort — the winner depends on data and language runtime:

- **Radix sorts** (e.g. `ska_sort`) are "almost always the fastest" on integer-like keys in compiled-language benchmarks — [Morwenn/cpp-sort wiki Benchmarks](https://github.com/Morwenn/cpp-sort/wiki/Benchmarks)
- **PDQsort** (pattern-defeating quicksort) is the fastest general-purpose *comparison* sort, combining quicksort's average case with heapsort's worst case and linear time on patterned inputs — [orlp/pdqsort](https://github.com/orlp/pdqsort), [arXiv:2106.05123](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.05123), [Boost.Sort docs](https://www.boost.org/doc/libs/latest/libs/sort/doc/html/sort/single_thread/pdqsort.html)
- **Timsort** (what Python's `sorted()` uses) excels on real-world partially ordered data — [Advanced Sorting Algorithms Benchmark](https://darshanjoshi.tech/projects/sorting-algorithms-benchmark), ["Fastest Sorting Algorithm? It Depends"](https://djangoproject.in/blog/fastest-sorting-algorithm/)

## What I wrote and ran

`benchmark.py` in `/Users/a1-6/Mypro/genai/GenAI2OpenAI/temp/claude-workflow-pp6_zq_j/` implements a **LSD radix sort** (base-256, stable, handles negatives via min-shift) and compares it against `sorted()` on 10 defined inputs plus 200 fuzz cases. Correctness is asserted against `sorted()` exactly, including input non-mutation. Output:

```
All correctness checks passed (10 defined inputs + 200 fuzz cases).

           input |       n |   radix_sort |     sorted() | ratio
------------------------------------------------------------------------
            pair |       2 |      0.01 ms |      0.00 ms |  92.1x
   all_equal_10k |   10000 |      0.21 ms |      0.07 ms |   2.9x
      sorted_20k |   20000 |      2.67 ms |      0.09 ms |  29.4x
    reversed_20k |   20000 |      2.60 ms |      0.09 ms |  28.9x
      random_20k |   20000 |      5.36 ms |      1.69 ms |   3.2x
     random_100k |  100000 |     26.78 ms |    10.01 ms |   2.7x
  few_values_50k |   50000 |      4.00 ms |     2.64 ms |   1.5x
   negatives_20k |   20000 |      2.79 ms |     1.63 ms |   1.7x

SORT_BENCH_OK
```

(Times are best-of-3 `time.perf_counter()` wall time; the tiny inputs are included for correctness but are meaningless for timing.)

## Honest result

**`sorted()` won on every input.** My radix sort is O(n·k) with k≈4 byte passes, asymptotically better than Timsort's O(n log n), but it runs in interpreted Python while `sorted()` runs in compiled C — the constant-factor gap (~30–100x) swamps the asymptotic advantage. This matches the search findings: radix sort's speed edge is real in C/C++/Rust, but in Python the quickest practical sort **is `sorted()` itself** (C-implemented Timsort/Powersort, with binary-insertion + Galloping merge). The script still prints `SORT_BENCH_OK` since all correctness checks passed and timings were measured as requested.
